▶️ Introduction: what a video platform must do

Hinglish samajh: YouTube bahut bada platform hai: lagbhag 2 billion monthly users, roz 5 billion videos dekhi jaati hain. Video ki files bahut badi hoti hain aur log turant aur bina ruke play hone ki ummeed karte hain. Isliye design ko paanch cheezon ka dhyan rakhna hota hai: tez upload, smooth streaming, video quality badalne ki suvidha, kam kharcha, aur high availability. Mukhya vichar: original upload ko blob storage mein rakho, har video ko kai formats mein transcode karo, aur CDN se dikhao.

YouTube is one of the biggest websites in the world. People upload videos, and billions of others watch them on phones, laptops and smart TVs. The chapter quotes some numbers (from 2020) to show the scale: about 2 billion monthly active users, 5 billion videos watched per day, 37% of mobile internet traffic coming from YouTube, availability in 80 languages, and 15.1 billion dollars of ad revenue in 2019. Even if you design for a much smaller platform, these numbers show what "video at scale" can look like.

Video is unusual because the files are huge and people expect them to play instantly and smoothly, without stopping to load, even on a slow connection. So the design must care about five things: fast video uploads, smooth video streaming, the ability to change video quality (low quality on a poor network, high quality on a good one), low infrastructure cost (storing and sending video is very expensive) and high availability and reliability.

The big ideas that the chapter develops are: store the original upload in blob storage, transcode (convert) each video into several formats and resolutions, deliver videos through a CDN that sits close to the viewers, and use a pipeline of parallel tasks to process videos quickly.

Scale of YouTube (2020 figures from the notes)

StatisticValue
Monthly active users2 billion
Videos watched per day5 billion
Share of mobile internet traffic37%
Languages80
Ad revenue in 201915.1 billion dollars

✨ Features

  • Upload videos and watch videos at massive scale.
  • Supports mobile apps, web browsers and smart TVs.
  • Needs fast uploads, smooth streaming and low cost.

✅ Benefits

  • A rich example of storage, processing and delivery at scale.
  • Reuses ideas from CDN, queues and blob storage.
  • Shows trade-offs between quality, speed and cost.

⚠️ Problems

  • Video storage and bandwidth are very expensive.
  • Processing each video is slow and heavy.
  • Users expect instant playback on any network.

YouTube is a massive video streaming platform supporting video uploads, playback, and various interactions. This chapter focuses on designing a scalable video streaming system with the following core features:

  • Fast video uploads
  • Smooth video streaming
  • Ability to change video quality
  • Low infrastructure cost

  • 2 billion monthly active users

Interview questions and answers

What are the main goals of a video platform design?
Fast uploads, smooth streaming, adjustable quality, low infrastructure cost, and high availability and reliability.
Why is video harder than text or images?
Files are huge, so storage, bandwidth and processing are expensive, and viewers need smooth playback on very different devices and networks.
Cross question: What are the biggest costs?
Bandwidth for streaming (CDN) and storage for the videos, so most optimizations target those.
Cross question: Why change video quality?
Networks differ. A low bitrate version avoids buffering on a weak connection, while a high bitrate version looks better on a fast one.

📝 Step 1: Scope, assumptions and cost

Hinglish samajh: Scope: video upload karna aur video dekhna, mobile app, web browser aur smart TV par. Maanyatayein: 5 million DAU, average video 300 MB, upload ki seema 1 GB. Meri maanyata ke hisaab se agar 10% users roz ek video upload karein to 500,000 x 300 MB = 150 TB per din storage. CDN ka kharcha: 5 million x 5 videos x 0.3 GB x 0.02 dollar = 150,000 dollar per din, isliye kharcha ghatane ke tareeke zaroori hain.

We keep the scope small: two core features, upload videos and watch videos. The service runs on mobile apps, web browsers and smart TVs. The assumptions are: 5 million daily active users (DAU), an average video size of 300 MB, and a maximum upload size of 1 GB. The notes also give a daily storage need of 150 TB and a CDN cost estimate.

Where does 150 TB come from? One way to reach it (this assumption is mine): if 10% of the 5 million daily users upload one video a day, that is 500,000 videos, and 500,000 x 300 MB = 150,000,000 MB = 150 TB per day. This is before storing several transcoded versions, which multiplies the storage again.

The CDN cost is the real eye-opener. Videos are streamed from a CDN, which charges for data transfer. With 5 million users each watching 5 videos a day of 0.3 GB at a price of 0.02 dollars per GB (using Amazon CloudFront pricing), the daily cost is 5,000,000 x 5 x 0.3 GB x 0.02 = 150,000 dollars per day. That is more than 4.5 million dollars a month, and it explains why the chapter spends time on cost-saving optimizations such as serving only popular videos from the CDN.

🧱 Step 2: High-level design: the components

Hinglish samajh: Sab kuch khud banana samajhdari nahi, isliye cloud ke blob storage (jaise S3) aur CDN ka use karte hain. Components: client, CDN, API servers (streaming ke alawa sab kaam), metadata database aur cache, original storage (raw uploads), transcoding servers (kai formats mein badalte hain), transcoded storage aur completion queue (transcoding khatam hone ki khabar). API traffic aur video traffic ko alag rakhna ek zaroori faisla hai.

It is not wise to build everything ourselves: for storage and delivery we should use existing cloud services (the cost and the effort of building a global video network are enormous). The design therefore uses a CDN and blob storage (such as Amazon S3).

The components are: the client (a phone, computer or TV that watches or uploads videos); the CDN, which stores and streams videos from servers close to the viewers; the API servers, which handle everything except streaming (feed recommendation, generating upload URLs, updating the metadata database and cache, user signup and so on); the metadata database and metadata cache, which store video details such as title, description, size, resolution and the uploader; original storage, a blob storage system for the raw uploaded videos; transcoding servers, which convert each video into multiple resolutions and formats; transcoded storage, a blob storage for the converted videos; and completion queue and handler, which carry the news "transcoding is finished" back to the system so metadata can be updated.

Keeping API traffic (small, frequent requests) separate from video traffic (large, heavy streams) is an important decision: the API servers are ordinary web servers, while video streaming is delivered straight from the CDN edge servers.

Components and jobs

ComponentJob
ClientPhone, computer or smart TV used to watch or upload
CDNStores and streams video from servers near the viewer
API serversEverything except streaming: upload URLs, metadata updates, feeds, signup
Metadata database and cacheVideo details: title, description, size, resolution, uploader
Original storageBlob storage for the raw uploaded videos
Transcoding serversConvert videos into many formats and resolutions
Transcoded storageBlob storage for converted videos
Completion queue and handlerTell the system that transcoding is done so metadata can be updated

✨ Features

  • Use cloud blob storage and a CDN instead of building them.
  • API servers handle everything except streaming.
  • Transcoding servers prepare videos for every device.

✅ Benefits

  • Much faster to build than doing everything ourselves.
  • Streaming scales through the CDN.
  • Each component has one job.

⚠️ Problems

  • Depends on the pricing and reliability of cloud providers.
  • The pipeline has several stages that can fail.
  • Metadata and video storage must stay consistent.

Name the main components of the video platform.
Clients, CDN, API servers, metadata database and cache, original storage, transcoding servers, transcoded storage and a completion queue with a handler.
Why separate video streaming from API servers?
Video is huge and best delivered by the CDN. The API servers stay lightweight and handle small requests.

It is cheaper and faster than building a global video delivery network, and these services already scale and replicate data.

⬆️ The video uploading flow

Hinglish samajh: Upload do hisson mein parallel hota hai: video file upload aur metadata update. Video upload: [1] original storage mein, [2] transcoding servers kai formats mein convert karte hain, [3] khatam hone par [3a] transcoded storage mein jaata hai aur [3b] completion queue mein event jaata hai; [3a.1] video CDN tak pahunchta hai aur [3b.1] completion handler metadata update karke user ko batata hai. Metadata update (file name, size, format) client alag se parallel bhejta hai.

Uploading has two parts that run in parallel: uploading the video file and updating its metadata. They are independent, so doing them at the same time makes the upload feel faster.

Video upload. [1] The video is uploaded to original storage (blob storage). [2] The transcoding servers fetch the video and convert it into several formats. [3] When transcoding is complete, two steps run in parallel: [3a] the transcoded videos are sent to transcoded storage, and [3b] a transcoding-completed event is put in the completion queue. [3a.1] The transcoded videos are then distributed to the CDN. [3b.1] The completion handler, which is a group of workers that read events from the completion queue, updates the metadata database and cache, and the user is told that the video is ready.

Metadata update. While the file is uploading, the client in parallel sends a request to update the video metadata: file name, size, format and so on. The API servers update the metadata cache and database. The title and description can be edited even while the video is still processing.

How it works, step by step

  1. [1] The video is uploaded to original (blob) storage.
  2. [2] Transcoding servers convert the video into several formats.
  3. [3] When transcoding is done, two things happen in parallel: [3a] transcoded videos go to transcoded storage; [3b] a completion event goes to the completion queue.
  4. [3a.1] The transcoded videos are distributed to the CDN.
  5. [3b.1] The completion handler updates the metadata and informs the user.

✨ Features

  • File upload and metadata update run in parallel.
  • Transcoding after the upload.
  • Completion queue and handler update status.

✅ Benefits

  • Fast perceived upload.
  • Decoupled stages that can be scaled separately.
  • Users are told when the video is ready.

⚠️ Problems

  • Transcoding takes time, so the video is not immediately watchable in all formats.
  • Failures between stages need retries.
  • The upload and the metadata must stay consistent.

Interview questions and answers

Describe the video upload flow.
The client uploads the video to original storage; transcoding servers convert it; the results go to transcoded storage and then the CDN; a completion event updates metadata and informs the user. In parallel, the client updates the metadata.
Why do upload and metadata update run in parallel?
They are independent, so running them together saves time and keeps the interface responsive.
Cross question: What if transcoding fails?
The job is retried from stored intermediate data. If the video is malformed, the system stops and returns an error code to the user.
Cross question: Why use a completion queue?
It decouples the transcoding step from the metadata update, so slow handlers do not block transcoding and events are not lost.

📺 The video streaming flow

Hinglish samajh: Streaming matlab video poori download hone se pehle hi chhote tukdon mein chalna shuru ho jaata hai. Humare design mein video seedha CDN ke sabse paas wale edge server se aata hai. Protocols (MPEG-DASH, Apple HLS, Adobe HDS) tay karte hain ki video kaise tukdon mein bata jaye aur player quality kaise badle. Alag devices ke liye alag protocols aur encodings chalte hain.

Streaming means that the video starts playing while it is still being downloaded in small pieces, instead of waiting for the whole file. This is what lets you click a video and see it start in a second, and what lets you skip forward without downloading everything before that point.

In our design, videos are streamed directly from the CDN, from the edge server closest to the viewer. This keeps the delay very small and keeps the heavy traffic off our own API servers. Different streaming protocols control how the video is split into chunks and delivered: the notes list MPEG-DASH, Apple HLS and Adobe HDS (Microsoft Smooth Streaming is another one). Different protocols support different video encodings and players, so when you design a streaming service you must choose a protocol that fits your clients.

The player usually switches quality on its own. It starts with a lower quality so playback begins fast, measures the network speed, and moves to a higher or lower quality chunk by chunk. This works only because we created several resolutions and bitrates during transcoding.

Streaming protocols mentioned in the notes

ProtocolOwner or originNote
MPEG-DASHOpen standard (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP)Widely supported adaptive streaming
HLSApple (HTTP Live Streaming)Required for many Apple devices
HDSAdobe (HTTP Dynamic Streaming)Older protocol

✨ Features

  • Videos are streamed straight from the CDN edge.
  • Protocols such as MPEG-DASH and HLS split videos into chunks.
  • Players switch quality as the network changes.

✅ Benefits

  • Playback starts quickly.
  • API servers carry no video traffic.
  • Viewers on slow networks still get smooth playback.

⚠️ Problems

  • Different devices need different protocols and encodings.
  • CDN bandwidth is the largest cost.
  • Edge caches must be warmed for new popular videos.

  • Some of te popular streaming protocols are MPEG_DASH, Apple HLS, Adobe HDS.

Interview questions and answers

How is video streamed to viewers?
Directly from the nearest CDN edge server, in small chunks over a streaming protocol such as MPEG-DASH or HLS.
What is a streaming protocol?
A standard that defines how a video is divided into chunks and delivered, so players can start quickly and change quality while playing.
Cross question: How does the player pick the quality?
It measures the download speed of recent chunks and requests the next chunk at a higher or lower bitrate to avoid buffering.
Cross question: Why not stream from our own servers?
It would add distance, load and cost. The CDN is designed to deliver large content close to users.

🎞️ Deep dive: video transcoding and the DAG model

Hinglish samajh: Transcode isliye karte hain: raw video bahut badi hoti hai (storage bachane ke liye), alag devices alag formats chalate hain, aur network ke hisaab se quality chahiye. Container (jaise MP4) video, audio aur metadata ko pakadta hai, aur codec (jaise H.264, VP9) compression karta hai. Kaam ko DAG (directed acyclic graph) mein banta jaata hai: video, audio aur metadata alag hote hain, phir video encoding, thumbnail, watermark aur audio encoding parallel chalte hain aur aakhir mein merge ho jaate hain.

Why transcode (convert) a video at all? The notes give three reasons. A raw video takes huge space: an hour of high definition raw video can be hundreds of gigabytes, so we compress it. Many devices and browsers support only certain formats, so we need several formats. And network conditions vary, so we deliver higher quality to users on fast networks and lower quality to those on slow ones, which also helps the video play smoothly.

Two terms are important. A container is the "basket" that holds the video file, the audio and the metadata; you recognize it by the file extension, such as .mp4, .avi or .mov. A codec is the compression and decompression algorithm that reduces the video size while keeping quality, for example H.264, VP9 or HEVC. A video file = container + codecs.

Transcoding is computationally expensive and takes time, and creators want different things (thumbnails, watermarks, different resolutions). To support this flexibility and high parallelism, the notes use a directed acyclic graph (DAG) model: a graph where each node is a task and each arrow means "this task must finish before the next one starts", and where there are no loops. The original video is first split into video, audio and metadata. Then tasks run on the parts, in parallel where possible: video encodings (convert to different resolutions, codecs and bitrates), thumbnail generation (uploaded by the user or generated automatically), watermark (an image overlay with identifying information such as a logo), and the audio is encoded separately. At the end the pieces are merged into the final video files.

Container vs codec

TermWhat it isExamples
ContainerHolds the video, audio and metadataMP4, AVI, MOV
CodecCompression and decompression algorithmH.264, VP9, HEVC

Why transcode

ReasonExplanation
Save spaceRaw video is huge; compression reduces it a lot
CompatibilityDifferent devices and browsers support different formats
Adapt to the networkDeliver higher quality on fast networks and lower quality on slow ones

✨ Features

  • Container plus codecs describe a video file.
  • A DAG defines tasks and their order.
  • Video, audio and metadata are processed separately.

✅ Benefits

  • High parallelism: independent tasks run at the same time.
  • Flexible: creators can define their own tasks.
  • Every device and network gets a suitable version.

⚠️ Problems

  • Transcoding is CPU-heavy and slow.
  • Many output versions multiply storage.
  • Complex pipelines need careful scheduling and retries.

Interview questions and answers

Why do we transcode videos?
To reduce storage, to support many devices and browsers, and to deliver the right quality for each network.
What are a container and a codec?
A container (such as MP4) holds video, audio and metadata. A codec (such as H.264 or VP9) compresses and decompresses the video.
What is the DAG model used for?
It defines the transcoding tasks and their dependencies, so independent tasks (video encoding, thumbnail, watermark, audio) can run in parallel.
Cross question: What is a watermark and why add it?

🏭 Deep dive: the video transcoding architecture

Hinglish samajh: Transcoding architecture ke paanch hisse: preprocessor (video ko GOP tukdon mein todta hai, DAG banata hai aur retry ke liye data temporary storage mein rakhta hai), DAG scheduler (DAG ko stages mein todkar tasks queue mein daalta hai), resource manager (task queue, worker queue aur running queue, aur ek task scheduler jo task ko sahi worker se jodta hai), task workers (encoding, thumbnail, watermark) aur temporary storage. Aakhir mein encoded video milta hai.

The DAG tells us what to do. The transcoding architecture is the machine that does it. It has five parts. The preprocessor has four responsibilities: it splits the video into small pieces called GOPs (a Group of Pictures is a short segment of frames that can be decoded on its own); it supports GOP-aligned splitting for older clients that cannot handle other cuts; it generates the DAG from configuration files written by programmers (the config defines tasks like "encode 720p" and "make thumbnail"); and it caches the segments and metadata in temporary storage, so that if encoding fails, the system can use the stored data to retry.

The DAG scheduler splits the DAG into stages of tasks and puts them in the task queue of the resource manager. For example: in stage 1 the video is split into video, audio and metadata; in stage 2 the video is processed by two tasks, video encoding and thumbnail creation, while audio is encoded and the metadata is saved.

The resource manager manages the efficiency of resource use. It contains three queues and a task scheduler: the task queue is a priority queue of tasks to run; the worker queue is a priority queue with worker utilization information; the running queue holds the tasks that are currently running and the workers that run them. The task scheduler picks the best task and worker pair and tells that worker to run the task, and it moves the task from the task queue to the running queue (and back if it fails).

Task workers run the tasks defined in the DAG: encoding, thumbnails, watermarks and so on; different workers can be specialized for different tasks. Temporary storage holds intermediate data (metadata that is frequently accessed goes to memory, and video or audio data goes to blob storage); data is removed when the video is done. The encoded video is the final output of the pipeline, for example funny_720p.mp4.

The five parts

PartResponsibility
PreprocessorSplit into GOPs, generate the DAG from configuration, store segments and metadata temporarily for retries
DAG schedulerSplit the DAG into stages of tasks and put them in the task queue
Resource managerTask queue, worker queue, running queue and a task scheduler that matches tasks to workers
Task workersRun the tasks: encoding, thumbnail, watermark and so on
Temporary storageHold intermediate data (memory for metadata, blob storage for video and audio) until the job ends

✨ Features

  • Preprocessor, DAG scheduler, resource manager, task workers and temporary storage.
  • Three queues in the resource manager.
  • Intermediate data stored so tasks can be retried.

✅ Benefits

  • Scales by adding workers.
  • Failures only retry the failed task.
  • Resources are used efficiently through scheduling.

⚠️ Problems

  • Many moving parts to build and run.
  • Scheduling decisions affect cost and latency.
  • Temporary storage must be cleaned up.

Interview questions and answers

Describe the transcoding architecture.
A preprocessor splits the video and builds a DAG; a DAG scheduler turns it into stages of tasks; a resource manager with task, worker and running queues assigns tasks to workers; task workers execute; temporary storage keeps intermediate data; the output is the encoded video.
What is a GOP?
A Group of Pictures: a short independent segment of video frames. Splitting by GOP lets chunks be encoded in parallel.
Cross question: What are the three queues in the resource manager?
The task queue (tasks waiting), the worker queue (worker availability and utilization) and the running queue (tasks currently running and their workers).
Cross question: Why store intermediate data?
If a worker fails, the task can be retried from the saved data instead of starting the whole video again.

⚡ Speed optimizations: parallel uploads, upload centers and queues

Hinglish samajh: Speed ke liye teen optimizations: parallel video upload (video ko GOP ke hisaab se chhote chunks mein todkar parallel upload karna, fail hone par sirf wahi chunk dobara), upload centers ko users ke paas rakhna (CDN ko upload hub banana), aur modules ke beech message queues lagana taaki ek doosre ka intezaar na karna pade aur kaam parallel chale.

Speed matters at two places: how fast a creator can upload and how fast a video is ready to watch. The notes suggest three optimizations. Parallel video uploads: uploading a whole large video in one go is slow and fragile; if the connection breaks, you must start again. Instead, split the video into smaller chunks by GOP alignment and upload the chunks in parallel. If one chunk fails, only that chunk is retried, and the upload can resume. This makes the upload faster and more reliable.

Place upload centers close to users: another way to speed up uploads is to set up several upload centers around the world, and send each user to the nearest one. A CDN can even act as an upload point close to the user, so that the file travels a short distance and then moves over fast internal networks to the storage.

Build everything parallel with message queues: in a simple design each module waits for the previous module to finish (download, then encode, then upload). This tight coupling makes the process slow. Putting a message queue between modules loosely couples them: the encoding module no longer waits for the download module to finish its whole job; whatever is in the queue can be processed in parallel by many workers, which increases the overall speed.

Tight vs loose coupling

DesignHow modules workResult
Tight coupling (no queue)Each module waits for the previous module to finishSlow, one slow step blocks everything
Loose coupling (message queues)Modules read from and write to queues; many workers run in parallelFaster, and each stage scales on its own

✨ Features

  • Chunked, parallel, resumable uploads.
  • Upload centers close to users.
  • Message queues for loose coupling.

✅ Benefits

  • Much faster uploads, especially for large files.
  • Failures only cost a chunk, not the whole upload.
  • The pipeline scales stage by stage.

⚠️ Problems

  • Chunking and reassembly add complexity.
  • More upload centers mean more infrastructure.
  • Queues need monitoring to avoid hidden backlogs.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Speed Optimizations

  1. Parallel Video Uploads: Split videos into smaller chunks for faster, resumable uploads.
  1. Distributed Upload Centers: Use CDNs as upload hubs close to users.
  2. Parallel Processing: Decouple modules using message queues for high parallelism.

Interview questions and answers

How do you speed up large video uploads?
Split the video into chunks, upload them in parallel and resume failed ones; upload to the nearest center; use queues to process in parallel.
Why use a message queue between processing modules?
To decouple them so that each module works independently and in parallel, instead of waiting for the previous module to finish.
Cross question: What happens if one chunk upload fails?
Only that chunk is retried. The other chunks are already uploaded and are kept.
Cross question: How does a CDN help uploads?
It can act as an upload hub close to the user, shortening the distance the file travels over the public internet.

🔒 Safety optimizations: pre-signed URLs and protecting videos

Hinglish samajh: Safety ke liye pehle pre-signed URL: client API server se ek temporary signed URL leta hai aur usi se storage mein video upload karta hai, taaki sirf authorized log hi upload kar saken. Doosre, copyrighted videos ki suraksha: DRM (Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine), AES encryption aur visual watermarking (logo ya naam overlay).

Video platforms must make sure that only the right people upload, and that valuable content is not stolen. First, pre-signed upload URLs. Instead of letting anyone upload straight to the blob storage, the client first asks the API servers for a pre-signed URL, a special temporary link that gives permission to upload one object to one place. The steps: (1) the client makes an HTTP request to the API servers to get the pre-signed URL (which gives access to the storage object); (2) the API servers respond with the URL; (3) once the client receives the response, it uploads the video using that URL. Because the URL is signed and temporary, only authorized users can upload.

Second, protecting copyrighted videos. Three common options: DRM (digital rights management) systems such as Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine and Microsoft PlayReady, which control how and where the video can be played. AES encryption: encrypt the video and set an authorization policy, so the video is decrypted only when played by an authorized user. Visual watermarking: put an image overlay with identifying information (for example the company logo or the creator's name) on top of the video to discourage copying.

How it works, step by step

  1. The client asks the API servers for a pre-signed upload URL.
  2. The API servers check permissions and return a temporary signed URL.
  3. The client uploads the video to storage using the signed URL.

Ways to protect videos

MethodHow it worksExamples
DRMControls playback with licenses and secure playersApple FairPlay, Google Widevine, Microsoft PlayReady
AES encryptionEncrypt the video; decrypt only for authorized usersAES with an authorization policy
Visual watermarkingOverlay identifying information on the videoCompany logo, creator name

✨ Features

  • Pre-signed URLs for authorized uploads.
  • DRM, AES encryption and watermarks for content protection.
  • Temporary, limited permissions.

✅ Benefits

  • Only authorized users can upload.
  • Content owners can protect their videos.
  • The upload path does not expose storage credentials.

⚠️ Problems

  • DRM adds cost and complexity and can limit device support.
  • Encryption and licensing need key management.
  • Watermarks can degrade the viewing experience slightly.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Safety Optimizations

  1. Pre-Signed URLs: Restrict video uploads to authorized users.
  1. Protect Videos:
    • DRM Systems (e.g., Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine).
    • AES Encryption.
    • Watermarking.

Interview questions and answers

What is a pre-signed URL and why use it?
A temporary signed link that allows uploading to storage. It ensures that only authorized users can upload, without exposing storage credentials.
How can you protect a video from copying?
Use DRM systems (FairPlay, Widevine, PlayReady), AES encryption with an authorization policy, and visual watermarks.
Cross question: Does DRM make copying impossible?
No, but it makes it much harder, and combined with encryption and watermarks it deters most abuse.
Cross question: Why not let clients upload with a permanent key?
A permanent key could leak and be abused. Pre-signed URLs expire and have narrow permissions.

💰 Cost-saving optimizations

Hinglish samajh: Kharcha ghatane ke tareeke video ki popularity ke "long tail" par based hain: kuch hi videos bahut dekhi jaati hain. (1) Sirf popular videos CDN se dikhao aur baaki apne high-capacity servers se; (2) kam dekhi jaane wali videos ko on-demand encode karo; (3) kuch videos sirf kuch regions mein popular hoti hain, unhe wahi rakho; (4) bahut bade platforms apna CDN banate hain aur ISPs ke saath partnership karte hain.

Remember the CDN bill of about 150,000 dollars per day. Cost is a main design driver, and the notes list four ways to reduce it. They rely on a common property of video: popularity follows a long-tail pattern. A small number of videos are watched very often, and the vast majority are rarely watched.

1. Serve only popular videos from the CDN, and others from our own high-capacity storage servers. The CDN is expensive, so we put on it only the videos that are watched a lot. Less popular videos can be served from our own servers, which cost less per gigabyte. 2. Encode short or rarely watched videos on demand instead of creating many versions in advance, which saves encoding compute and storage. 3. Some videos are popular only in certain regions, so there is no need to distribute them worldwide; keep them in the regions where they are watched. 4. Build your own CDN and partner with Internet Service Providers (ISPs), as big companies do, because building your own CDN is a huge project but can save a lot on bandwidth for the biggest players.

Cost saving ideas

IdeaWhy it saves money
Popular videos on the CDN, others on our own serversCDN bandwidth is expensive, and only popular videos need it
Encode rarely watched videos on demandAvoids producing and storing versions that nobody watches
Distribute by regionDo not copy a video to regions where nobody watches it
Own CDN with ISP partnershipsReduces per-GB bandwidth cost at very large scale

✨ Features

  • Use the long-tail pattern of video popularity.
  • Encode on demand and distribute regionally.
  • Own CDN with ISPs for the biggest platforms.

✅ Benefits

  • Large savings on bandwidth, the largest cost.
  • Less storage for unwatched versions.
  • Better use of expensive CDN capacity.

⚠️ Problems

  • Videos served from our own servers may start slower.
  • On-demand encoding adds delay for the first viewer.
  • Predicting popularity takes analytics.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Cost-Saving Optimizations

  1. Serve only popular videos via CDN; less popular ones from high-capacity servers.
  2. Encode on-demand for rarely accessed videos.
  3. Regionalize video distribution based on popularity.
  4. Build custom CDNs and partner with ISPs to reduce bandwidth costs.

Interview questions and answers

How would you reduce the cost of a video platform?
Serve only popular videos from the CDN and the rest from cheaper servers, encode rare videos on demand, distribute by region, and for huge scale build your own CDN with ISP partnerships.
Why does the long tail matter?
Most videos are rarely watched, so paying for premium delivery for all of them is wasteful.
Cross question: What is the downside of on-demand encoding?
The first viewer may wait longer, so use it only for rarely watched videos where the trade-off is acceptable.
Cross question: How would you decide which videos are "popular"?
Track view counts and growth over time, and promote a video to the CDN when its views pass a threshold.

🛠️ Error handling and final revision

Hinglish samajh: Errors do tarah ke hote hain: recoverable (jaise upload ya transcoding fail hona) jinhe dobara try karna chahiye, aur non-recoverable (jaise kharab video) jinhe rok kar error code lautana chahiye. Server fail hone par stateless servers dusre server par chale jaate hain, cache replicated hota hai, aur metadata master fail ho to slave ko master bana dete hain. Revision table mein poore chapter ka saar hai.

Large systems fail all the time, so error handling is a key part of the design. The notes divide errors into two types. Recoverable errors are temporary problems that can succeed if you try again: for example a video segment fails to transcode, a network call times out, or a worker is not available. The approach is to retry a few times (with delays), and if it keeps failing, return an error code to the client. Non-recoverable errors are permanent problems, such as a malformed video that cannot be decoded. The system should stop processing that video and return an appropriate error code.

Here are typical failures per component and the usual response (my summary of common practice, not from the repository notes): upload error (retry), split video error (if old clients cannot split by GOP, pass the whole video to the server for splitting), transcoding error (retry), preprocessor error (regenerate the DAG), DAG scheduler error (reschedule), resource manager queue down (use a replica), task worker down (retry the task on a new worker), API server down (stateless, so redirect to another API server), metadata cache server down (data is replicated, so read from another node and bring up a new one), metadata DB server down (if it is the master, promote a slave; if it is a slave, use another slave). Below is a compact summary and a revision sheet.

Error types

TypeExampleResponse
RecoverableFailed upload, transcoding timeout, no worker availableRetry; return an error code if it keeps failing
Non-recoverableMalformed videoStop processing and return an error code

Chapter revision

TopicKey point
Scale5M DAU, 300 MB videos, 150 TB per day, about 150,000 dollars per day of CDN cost
Upload flowOriginal storage, transcoding, transcoded storage and CDN, completion queue updates metadata
StreamingFrom the nearest CDN edge using MPEG-DASH, HLS or HDS
TranscodingContainer plus codecs, DAG tasks, preprocessor, scheduler, resource manager, workers

SafetyPre-signed URLs, DRM, AES encryption, watermarks

✨ Features

  • Retry for recoverable errors.
  • Stop and report for non-recoverable errors.
  • Replicas and stateless servers for failover.

✅ Benefits

  • Temporary failures do not lose work.
  • Bad input does not waste resources.
  • The system keeps serving other users during failures.

⚠️ Problems

  • Endless retries can add load, so cap retries.
  • Error codes must be clear to users.
  • Failover paths must be tested.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Error Handling

Recoverable Errors

  • Retry failed uploads, transcoding, or resource allocation tasks.

Non-Recoverable Errors

  • Stop malformed video processing and return error codes.

Interview questions and answers

Summarize the video platform design in one minute.
Clients upload to blob storage through pre-signed URLs; transcoding servers, scheduled with a DAG, produce many formats stored in transcoded storage and pushed to a CDN; viewers stream from the nearest CDN edge; metadata lives in a database with a cache; queues decouple the stages; cost is controlled by serving only popular videos via the CDN.
How do you handle errors?
Retry recoverable errors (upload, transcoding, resource allocation) and stop on non-recoverable errors such as malformed videos, returning an error code.
Cross question: What if the metadata master database fails?
Promote a replica (slave) to master, as in the replication design from chapter 1.
Cross question: What if a transcoding worker dies?
The resource manager reassigns the task to another worker, using the stored intermediate data.
